proofs.requirement: Lymphatic vessels collect tissue fluid and ultimately return it to blood; vessels transport and nodes are organized organs, not passive pipes.
proofs.sourceExcerpt: Fluid leaves small blood vessels and enters tissue. Lymphatic vessels collect part of that fluid, now called **lymph**, and ultimately return it to the blood. Lymph can carry dissolved material and migrating cells. Vessels are the transport routes; **lymph nodes** are organized organs along those routes.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A lymph node is organised immune tissue along lymphatic routes.

Lymph is interstitial fluid collected by lymph capillaries and returned to the venous blood (National Cancer Institute SEER training), so lymph and blood are different fluids and a sample of one does not stand in for the other.

proofs.sourceExcerpt: Some [dendritic cells](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/innate-and-unconventional-cells/dendritic-cells) collect antigen in tissue and migrate to a draining node. Sixt and colleagues demonstrated this earlier soluble-antigen route in mouse lymph nodes: it did not require every antigen to wait for a migrating DC.

proofs.requirement: One simplified blood branch connects arterial input through a capillary network to postcapillary HEV and venous output; blood lumens remain separate from lymph spaces. This is neither an artery-to-vein shortcut nor a complete exclusive vascular map.
proofs.sourceExcerpt: BLOOD CIRCUIT: At the hilar region show a distinct coral artery entering, a separate slate-blue vein leaving, and a separate sage-green efferent lymphatic leaving. Keep the three lumens visibly separate and nonintersecting. Label “Artery” and “Vein”; a coral arrow in the artery points INTO the node, a slate-blue arrow in the vein points OUT. Within the node, a modest thin-walled capillary arc connects the arterial branch to a postcapillary HEV segment in the T-cell region; the HEV continues into the venous outlet. Label the small connecting segment “Capillaries” and the specialized venous segment “HEV”. This is ONE simplified example of a branched blood network, not the only route, not an artery-to-vein bypass, and not a complete vascular map. All blood segments have closed endothelial walls. Neither artery, capillary, HEV nor vein opens into a lymph sinus or the efferent lymphatic. Red disc-shaped cells stay inside blood lumens. A small round circulating naive lymphocyte crosses FROM the HEV BLOOD LUMEN across the wall INTO NODE TISSUE, marked by one bold blue movement arrow. The arrow must start in blood and end in node tissue; it is not a blood-flow arrow and not a lymph-flow arrow. Do not draw every circulating cell crossing the wall, lymphocyte entry through the artery wall, reverse crossing or a universal bidirectional route. Both B and T lymphocytes can be represented; drawn cell colors/counts are schematic conventions, not measured biology.

proofs.requirement: Draining denotes tissue territory, not cancer involvement. Enlargement and imaging do not establish malignancy; pathologic involvement concerns examined tissue, and a sampled negative node does not certify unsampled nodes.
proofs.sourceExcerpt: Cancer cells can also travel in lymph. This possibility does not make every draining or enlarged node cancer-positive. **Pathologic involvement** means cancer was identified in examined tissue; it differs from an anatomical drainage route, immune-cell accumulation or an imaging observation. A sampled negative node does not certify every unsampled node. Breast-specific [regional anatomy](/wiki/education/concepts/breast-cancer/anatomy-and-histology/lymphatic-drainage-and-axilla) and [node assessment](/wiki/education/concepts/breast-cancer/surgery-and-pathology-results/sentinel-node-and-axillary-dissection) provide the next layer.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A lymph node is organised immune tissue along lymphatic routes. Nearby nodes can be among the earliest sites of spread for many cancers, but drainage does not establish cancer involvement. Nodal findings can inform staging according to the cancer-specific rules. Sentinel-node biopsy identifies and examines the first draining node or nodes. Removing fewer nodes is generally associated with fewer side effects, but sentinel-node biopsy can also cause lymphoedema. Nodes can support antitumour T-cell priming; antigen arrival alone does not establish that this occurred.

Pathological involvement means cancer was identified in examined tissue, which differs from a drainage route, enlargement or an imaging observation, and a negative sampled node does not certify the unsampled nodes (the National Cancer Institute notes that a false-negative biopsy gives a false sense of security about the extent of cancer).

Peripheral tolerance acts on mature cells in tissues and lymphoid organs.

Immune ignorance is a setting where the relevant cells have not effectively met the antigen, which is different from tolerance after an encounter, and an antibody concentration alone cannot show that self-reactive B cells were deleted or restrained.

proofs.sourceExcerpt: Teaching details: Locate the compartments before reading the outcome. Local signals near injured or stressed tissue can affect a nearby vessel and recruit circulating cells. The arrow across the vessel wall depicts **cell entry**, while the separate fluid/protein arrow depicts increased permeability. It does not depict a new vessel growing. Responders may support containment and repair; persistent signaling may accompany further injury. The sketch is schematic, with no measured time course or inevitable outcome, and infection is only one possible trigger. None of these tissue changes establishes tumor-specific recognition or useful cancer control. [Inflammation physiology](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18650913/)

proofs.requirement: Macrophage states depend on local signal combinations; M1/M2 are simplified experimental poles, not universal boxes for human tissue cells. Marker panels or RNA scores are not complete functional identities.
proofs.sourceExcerpt: Different **macrophage states** illustrate this complexity. Macrophages can respond to many combinations of local signals. The familiar M1/M2 labels describe simplified experimental poles, not two universal boxes that contain every human tissue macrophage. A marker panel or RNA score should not be turned into a complete functional identity.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: What a macrophage is doing depends on where it came from, where it sits, and the signals and history it has had, so the two-box labels M1 and M2 describe a laboratory comparison and not every macrophage in a tissue. In a tumour, a macrophage's label does not on its own show what it is doing to the cancer or to T cells.

In a tumour, a tumour-associated macrophage is named for its location, and its state and tested functions are separate questions. A tumour can hold several programmes in different neighbourhoods or at different times. An expression cluster can suggest a repair, interferon or lipid-handling programme, which is a hypothesis; it does not establish that the cells suppress T cells, kill cancer cells or would respond to a macrophage-directed drug. One marker such as CD163 does not establish a universal suppressive state, a change in proportions between two biopsies does not show that the same cells changed state, and the plain statement that M1 is good and M2 is bad loses the tissue and experiment that give a response its meaning.
CD163 is a receptor found on monocytes and macrophages. Detecting it alone does not establish a tumour-supporting function or benefit from a particular drug.

proofs.requirement: Woo and Bakhoum report context-dependent antitumor versus metastatic DNA-sensing mechanisms in different experimental systems, not a head-to-head clinical comparison.
proofs.sourceExcerpt: Inflammatory signaling can support immune recognition in one context and support tumor progression or tissue injury in another. Woo and colleagues found a DNA-sensing pathway supporting antitumor immune responses in defined tumor models. Bakhoum and colleagues found a cytosolic DNA response promoting metastatic behavior in different experimental cancer systems. These are contextual mechanisms, not a head-to-head clinical comparison.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In experimental cancer systems one DNA-sensing pathway has had opposite roles: host STING-dependent sensing was needed for spontaneous CD8 T-cell priming against mouse tumours (Woo et al., 2014), while a tumour-cell response to cytosolic DNA in chromosomally unstable tumours promoted metastasis (Bakhoum et al., 2018). These are contextual mechanisms and not a head-to-head clinical comparison.
